channel.title: Blowhorn Resources: Product intelligence
channel.description: Everything in Blowhorn Resources tagged Product intelligence.

item.title: Failed posts are data: reading failure reasons and fixing the cause
item.description: A failed post is a report, not just a red mark. The reason on the activity names the cause, and the fix follows from the reason: re-sign in, shrink the run, fix the content, or wait out the platform. Retry only after a fix, never in a loop.

item.title: Pace is a feature: typing delay, concurrency and approval gates
item.description: Speed feels like efficiency until a platform reads it as automation. Typing delay, concurrency and approval gates are the three dials that keep a fast schedule looking human, and each one trades a little time for a lot of safety.

item.title: The open web is closing. Show up where your audience is.
item.description: AI answers now reuse Reddit's posts without sending the click, and Reddit is answering with logins and its app. Here is what that shift means for anyone who builds an audience in public, and how to keep showing up in your own voice.

item.title: Your release, drafted by your assistant, fired by you
item.description: Your changelog already says what shipped. Here is how to have an assistant turn it into release posts for the networks your buyers read, queue them for a good hour, and still keep the decision to send in your own hands.

item.title: Why your assistant rehearses first
item.description: Every write through the Blowhorn MCP server is a dry run until you confirm. What a rehearsal shows, what to check before you say go, why an agent can never approve its own content, and what approval mode and secrets handling add.

item.title: Ship release notes everywhere your contributors read
item.description: A tagged release deserves notes written for each place your contributors read: Hacker News, GitHub, Reddit, Slack and Bluesky. Why channel-native wording beats pasting one post everywhere, and how to preview each before it goes out.

item.title: Let an agent rally the first hour without approving itself
item.description: Plan the first hour of a company post with your teammates' contributed profiles, let an agent queue the work, and keep a person in charge of approval. Why an agent can never approve its own content, and why that is the point.

item.title: Five minutes from ~/.local/bin/blowhorn-mcp to your first dry run
item.description: Open Blowhorn once, add one command to your assistant, check it connected, read something, then rehearse your first write as a dry run and confirm it. Short, exact steps for Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or Claude Desktop.

item.title: Agents across client brands, with a kill switch in your hand
item.description: If you run several brands, an assistant can save hours, and a mistake lands on someone else's name. One profile per client brand, risk limits per profile, a dry run per brand, and a way to pause everything with a reason.

item.title: Won or lost in the first hour
item.description: Feeds are widely believed to show a new post to a few people first and widen its reach only if they respond. Here is what that early test looks like, what each platform has and hasn't said about it, and how to schedule so the first hour has readers in it.

item.title: When a platform changes the rules
item.description: Posting limits shrink, formats change, and yesterday's healthy schedule starts failing. Here is how rule changes show up in your activity, how Blowhorn responds, and the three moves to make on your side.

item.title: The scheduling craft: spacing, timing and queues
item.description: Platforms do not judge your posts one at a time; they judge the shape of your activity. Spacing, timing and queue discipline are how a busy schedule still reads as one person posting at a human pace.

item.title: Reading your results: what a post's numbers tell you
item.description: A posted checkmark is the start of the information, not the end. Here is how to read the numbers on a finished activity, spot the three patterns that matter, and change one thing at a time.
